noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: describe the levels of organisation in organisms: organelles, cells, tissues, organs and systems

primer.text: You already know that living things are built from cells, and that a cell contains smaller working parts such as the nucleus. This lesson stacks those ideas into a ladder, showing how specialised parts nest inside one another from tiny organelles up to whole organ systems running an entire body.

lessons.title: From Cells to Organ Systems
lessons.opening: Every organism is assembled from cells, the smallest living building units. A single-celled organism manages with just one cell doing every job; larger organisms build upwards, because their cells specialise, and groups of specialists then team up into tissues, organs and finally organ systems that keep the whole body alive.
keyPoints: Unicellular organisms manage with one cell, while multicellular ones are built from many cooperating cells.
The nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes are among the organelles a cell houses.
Specialised cells join together to make a tissue.
Different tissues combine to build an organ.
Organs that share one overall job form an organ system — the top rung.

low.restatement: One cell grows into many, then tissues, organs and systems: each rung nests inside the next.
low.analogy: Like a book, where words make sentences, sentences make paragraphs, paragraphs make chapters and chapters make the book.
low.examPointer: When asked to describe the levels of organisation, name every rung of the ladder in the correct order.

medium.restatement: Specialisation drives the ladder — each level divides the work of survival a little further.
medium.analogy: Think of a hospital: individual staff, then wards, then departments, then the whole hospital.
medium.examPointer: Practise classifying named examples — a mitochondrion, muscle, the heart — at their correct level.

check.stem: Which level of organisation sits directly above cells in the hierarchy?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Organelles sit below cells — they are the parts inside one.
An organ is two rungs up, built from several tissues.
A system is the top rung, a team of organs.

options.text: A specialised structure inside a cell that carries out one particular job
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: A group of similar cells doing one job
options.explanation: That defines a tissue, not a cell part.

options.text: A structure built from several tissues
options.explanation: That is the definition of an organ.
Organelles are discrete structures, not the fluid around them.

check.stem: At which single level of organisation would the heart alone be placed?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The heart is not one repeated cell type; it contains muscle, nerve and connective tissues.
The heart alone is not a system — it is one member of the circulatory system.
The heart is far too large and complex to be a single cell.

check.stem: Which statement about unicellular organisms is correct?

options.text: Their single cell must carry out every life process the organism needs
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
That describes multicellular organisms.

options.text: They are built from tissues working together
options.explanation: Tissues require many cells; unicellular organisms have just one.
Even single cells house organelles such as the nucleus.

check.stem: Which sequence orders cell, tissue, organ and system by increasing complexity?

options.text: Cell, then tissue, then organ, then organ system
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Tissue, then cell, then organ, then organ system
options.explanation: A tissue cannot come before the cells that form it.

options.text: Cell, then organ, then tissue, then organ system
options.explanation: Organs are assembled from tissues, so tissue must come first.

options.text: Organ system, then organ, then tissue, then cell
options.explanation: That is the decreasing order, not increasing.

check.stem: Define a tissue in one sentence.
check.modelAnswer: A tissue is a group of similar cells working together to carry out one particular function.

check.stem: Name the five levels of organisation in order, starting with the smallest.
check.modelAnswer: Organelles, then cells, then tissues, then organs, then organ systems.

check.stem: Explain why multicellular organisms need specialised cells.
check.modelAnswer: Because a single unspecialised cell could not perform every job a whole body demands; specialisation lets each cell type become efficient at one task, and the different specialists then combine into tissues, organs and systems that divide the workload between them.

check.stem: A leaf is called an organ. Justify this by naming the level found directly below it.
check.modelAnswer: An organ is a structure assembled from several different tissues, and a leaf contains tissues such as mesophyll and epidermis working on one job; those tissues in turn consist of specialised leaf cells, so the level directly below the leaf organ is tissue.

lessons.title: Reading the Organisation Tables
sourceHeadings: Examples of Organ Systems in Animals & Plants Table
lessons.opening: Two reference tables pin the hierarchy down. The first defines what each level means, and the second maps real organ systems in animals and plants onto the organs and tissues inside them. Treat both as lookup charts when a classification question asks you to place a structure.
keyPoints: An organelle is a specialised structure within a cell that performs one specific function.
A tissue is a group of similar cells performing one particular function.
An organ combines different tissues to complete a specific job.
An organ system is a set of organs cooperating on one overall function.
Plant examples include the shoot system, whose organs include leaf, stem and flower.
The mitochondrion, site of aerobic respiration, illustrates an organelle at work.

low.restatement: The tables give a definition per level and a worked list of systems, organs and tissues.
low.analogy: Like a dictionary plus an atlas: one explains the terms, the other shows where they occur.
low.examPointer: Quote a definition word-for-word and attach a named example for full marks.

medium.restatement: Classification questions are answered by matching structure to the level whose definition it fits.
medium.analogy: Sorting mail: read the address (the structure), then file it in the right drawer (the level).
medium.examPointer: Learn one organ system from each kingdom — shoot or root for plants, circulatory for animals.

check.stem: Which organelle is named as the site of aerobic respiration?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The nucleus stores genetic material; respiration happens elsewhere.
Ribosomes build proteins, not respiration.
Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis in plant cells.

check.stem: Which organ system contains the leaf, stem and flower as its organs?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Roots and tubers belong to the root system.
That system handles trachea and lungs.
Lungs, kidneys and skin serve excretion.

check.stem: Xylem and phloem appear in the tissue column of both plant systems. What are they?

options.text: Tissues that transport substances around the plant
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
They are listed in the tissue column, below the organ level.
They are macroscopic structures, not cell parts.
A single transport tissue is not a whole system.

check.stem: The digestive, circulatory and respiratory systems share which tissue examples?

options.text: Muscle, connective, nerve and epithelial tissues
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Those are plant transport tissues.
Those belong to leaves.
Those are leaf structures, not the listed tissue set.

check.stem: Which pairing of system to organs is correct according to the table?

options.text: Excretory system — lungs, kidneys and skin
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
The nervous system lists brain and spinal cord.
The circulatory system lists the heart.
Ovary, uterus and testes belong to reproduction.

check.stem: State the definition of an organ system given in the table.
check.modelAnswer: A set of organs cooperating on one overall function — that is the table's definition.

check.stem: Name two organs of the root system and one tissue found in it.
check.modelAnswer: The root and the tuber are its organs, and xylem or phloem are tissues found there.

check.stem: Explain why the heart is listed as an organ rather than a tissue.
check.modelAnswer: Because the heart is built from several different tissues — muscle, connective, nerve and epithelial — cooperating on one job, and an organ is exactly that combination, whereas a tissue would be many similar cells of one type.

check.stem: A surgeon biopsies a small patch of stomach muscle. Place the sample, the stomach and digestion in order of organisational level.
check.modelAnswer: The sample of muscle is a tissue, the stomach is an organ built from tissues, and digestion is carried out by the digestive system, a group of cooperating organs.

glossary.definition: A specialised structure inside a cell that carries out one particular job, such as the mitochondrion.
A group of similar cells working together on one particular function.
A structure built from several different tissues cooperating on a specific task.
A set of organs that work together to carry out one overall function.

workedExample.prompt: A diagram labels three structures: 1 a whole leaf, 2 a section through the leaf, 3 a single cell taken from a layer of the leaf. A table offers possible categorisations. Which option assigns each label to its correct level of organisation?
steps: Label 1 is the entire leaf, a structure assembled from several tissues, so it is an organ.
Label 2 is a single palisade mesophyll cell.
Label 3 is the upper epidermis, a layer of similar cells doing one job, which makes it a tissue.
Only option B matches all three assignments.
workedExample.finalAnswer: B — 1 is the leaf organ, 2 is a palisade mesophyll cell and 3 is the upper epidermis.
